does this represent a bug in the migration?
It indicates a migration-path bug or an incompatible old cache being admitted to that path. I’ll check which—the fresh-store fallback recovers the run, but doesn’t explain the missing table.

Yes—an upgrade-compatibility bug from the migration renumbering.

The old cache reports version 39, but its schema matches this branch’s former native-resolution migration 39. After the master merge, version 39 means a different schema containing policy tables. The upgrader has no bridge for that old lineage, so it reaches migration 41 and tries to drop a table that never existed.

The original cache remains intact. The fresh-store fallback worked, but we wasted the upgrade time because that incompatibility wasn’t detected before copying and migrating.

For M2, I’ve settled the local/parameter projection gap: retain producer-owned declaration kind and spelling on the canonical source declaration, then project through its exact identity. Storage is now a fourth isolated lane; I’m implementing the shared metadata API and selected-operation wiring.

The producer, result-status, and typed-metadata changes are integrated for validation. Review found two follow-ups: rendering could still turn a cancelled result into “resolved,” and the typed tests needed stronger reuse/cancellation checks. Those are running in parallel.

The exact workload also exposed a publication limit: one legitimate Rust file exceeds the 400,000-row write cap with native facts. I’m checking that contract before changing it.

Canonical local/parameter storage and projection are now integrated, including the type request’s one-session path. I’m adding the indexed-read regression and preparing the combined test run. The remaining adapter lane is exercising these results through lookup outcomes without switching production routing.

The combined build is running. I also found and fixed a prerequisite for type lookup: ordinary bare value/type references had binding facts but no type projections. They now emit structured projections; generic and `Self` uncertainty remains explicit.

Yes. The old cache’s version number was reused for a different migration lineage, so the upgrader chose an incompatible migration. The original cache is preserved, but the failed upgrade wasted time before falling back to a fresh store.

M2 validation has also exposed several stale expectations and a few issues to investigate; I’m collecting and fixing those together before another build.

The combined gate finished: 2,426 passed, nine failed. One failure exposed missing declared-type facts for constants/statics; another was a migration-test fixture with colliding blob IDs. I’ve also guarded async calls against incorrectly reporting their awaited output type. These fixes and the native point/type adapter will go through the next build together.

The native point/type adapter is integrated but still test-only. Review caught one more correctness issue: ambiguity must be counted from canonical declaration identities, even when their displayed definitions collapse to the same value. That is corrected; production routing remains unchanged.

The next combined build is running. The normal-cache diagnostic is also still running; it has not produced the required partition yet. Its oversized-publication warnings alone don’t establish a query failure, so I’m leaving that run intact.

The new adapter tests are running. Most have passed so far; the dirty-overlay fixture returned `Unavailable`, which I’m investigating. The async reverse-completion fixture also had a stale source-position selector; that test setup is corrected.

The overlay result was correct: the fixture supplied new source without preparing its canonical facts. I’ve updated it to check both states—`Unavailable` before preparation, then the exact overlay definition afterward. No resolver fallback was added.

The gate finished at 2,442 passed and two failed, both fixture setup issues now corrected. The 1,024-mount scale check also passed with unchanged SQL and work counts. I’m starting confirmation with the additional `self`, async-definition, and type-cancellation fixtures included.

All three scale checks passed—256, 1,024, and 2,048 mounts—with unchanged work counts. The full confirmation build is underway. The remaining major M2 gate is still the exact `missing_tests` partition; scale results do not substitute for it.
Compilation is still running. The fixes are checkpointed, and I’m holding further source changes until this gate finishes.

Confirmation found one remaining producer issue: the async result-type gap was also being marked as missing reference coverage, making reverse lookup unnecessarily incomplete. I’ve restricted it to typing; the existing reverse-binding test will verify that distinction.

The latest gate passed 2,444 of 2,445 tests; the async coverage fix is ready. Before rebuilding, I’m checking one final point-lookup boundary: supplied source text must match the selected file, even if its byte offsets happen to match. Otherwise a stale buffer could resolve against the wrong source.

The next combined gate is running with the async fix and source-identity check. Rust’s fact version is now v39, so cached draft facts won’t survive these producer corrections. Production routing is still unchanged.

Independent review confirmed the source-mismatch bug and the guard: public lookup APIs accept caller-supplied text without guaranteeing it matches indexed content. The fix uses existing content identities and preserves the selected operation’s final freshness check.
The current 2,446-test run has reported no failures so far. The historical diagnostic is still publishing the normal cache, so I’m leaving that process intact.

All 2,446 tests passed. The native point/type adapters, lexical source metadata, async completion separation, and source-identity guard are validated.

M2 is still awaiting the exact `missing_tests` partition. The normal-cache diagnostic remains in progress; M3 production routing has not started.

The implementation gate is green. Formatting found only a module-ordering change, now corrected. I’m waiting on the normal-cache diagnostic before moving to the exact-workload gate; no new Rust build is running.

The cache upgrade has already finished; the remaining process is building facts with the older v35 binary. Now that v39 has passed validation, that old run cannot certify the current code.

I’m stopping only the obsolete diagnostic and restarting it with the validated binary against the normal cache. No cache deletion or temporary cache.

While the cache work runs, I’m preparing native call-result projection fixtures in another Optane worktree. This will check exact call sites, owners, arguments, and incomplete evidence without switching production routes.

Yes—the schema-v39 collision is a cache migration bug: the upgrader assumed two different schema histories were compatible. The original cache was preserved, but the failed upgrade wasted substantial time. Separately, I’m checking the diagnostic executable’s provenance before counting its results toward M2.

The executable is current: it contains the new source-identity regression. The missing v111 filename is expected while the normal upgrader migrates its staged copy of v109 before publishing it. I’ll let that finish. The parallel incoming-call projection work is also ready for review.

Review caught a source-consistency issue in the call projection: it must read call syntax inside the selected operation, so final revalidation covers both the resolved target and its source ranges. I’m also checking the bounded forward-query API needed for outgoing calls and broad graphs before changing any production routes.

The call-projection fixtures are integrated and compiling in a focused run. They cover free/member calls, ambiguity, source ranges, and cancellation. The migration review hasn’t found a missing-index cascade so far. The current v109→v111 upgrade removes obsolete derived facts and checks database integrity; that cost is separate from the confirmed old-v39 schema-history bug. I’m leaving the normal upgrade running.

The forward-query audit found a reusable path: broad graphs already have file-major native batches, and outgoing calls can share the existing selected read session. The call-fixture run found a test setup error—a top-level Rust function still has a module owner—which is corrected; confirmation is running.

Both new call-projection tests now pass. The parallel forward-session implementation is also ready for review; it lets several native call lookups share one selected context and fact-read session. The exact workload is still waiting on the normal cache upgrade.

Yes—the `policy_unit_reads` failure is a migration-compatibility bug.

Two different schema histories used version **39**. The upgrader treated the old native-resolution cache as belonging to the merged history, copied it, then ran a migration requiring tables it never contained.

We should detect that lineage before copying and either migrate it correctly or explicitly rebuild. The original cache is preserved; the defect is documented but not fixed.

The current v109→v111 upgrade’s slowness is separate—not yet evidence of another correctness bug.
fix it and finish M2/M3

The migration fix is underway in an isolated worktree. I’ve also integrated the forward-session and inventory tests; next I’ll validate them together with outgoing-call projection while preparing the remaining consumer routes.

The cache fix can preserve existing data: the old v39 schema matches a known set of native migrations, so it can be bridged into the merged chain.

Separately, the current v109→v111 upgrade has used over two hours of CPU and is still in SQLite. I’m checking where that time is going while consumer work continues.

The lineage bridge now reproduces the merged schema in standalone SQLite checks; its preservation regressions are ready for review.

I also confirmed the separate long-running upgrade is stuck in migration 110’s native-interior deletion, not schema validation. That points to deletion cost, so I’m examining its cascades before treating this as normal upgrade time.

The decision is recorded in the ExecPlan, including the Optane override. Startup is being changed to reject pre-native caches before copying them and rebuild an old cache if it appears under the active filename. Caches created after the reset will still be reused on subsequent opens.

The startup reset is implemented: old-version candidates are rejected before any copy, and an old schema under the active filename is rebuilt under the SQLite write lock. I’m checking the reset and reopen tests now; branch validation will use only the dedicated Optane root.

The new startup tests pass: old caches are not imported, an old active database is reset, and a native cache retains its data on reopen.

The full core run found 20 historical migration tests still calling production startup. I’m separating those fixtures from startup so they don’t contradict the new reset policy.

All 519 core tests now pass. Schema 112 enforces the fresh-start boundary, and pre-native caches cannot be imported. The decision and `BIFROST_CACHE_ROOT=/mnt/optane/bifrost-cache-2771` isolation rule are recorded. I’m returning to M2/M3 validation with that policy in place.

The current batch covers incoming calls with full resolution evidence, native broad-graph projection, rename capture checks, and corrected Rust inventory gaps. Yes—existing pre-2771 cache contents will be replaced, not migrated. I’ll use `BIFROST_CACHE_ROOT=/mnt/optane/bifrost-cache-2771` for local validation and leave other agents’ caches untouched until we push to master.

The fresh-start cache gate passed all 519 core tests. The broader M2/M3 batch passed 2,467 of 2,472: three failures concern reference-inventory expectations, and two tests incorrectly assume no cache-root override. I’ve delegated the inventory investigation and am fixing those two tests before the next batched run.

The inventory bug was a duplicate AST visit: a method name already emitted as a reference was later marked “unlowered.” That is corrected, with unsupported field reads still reported honestly. The same broad gate is rebuilding now; production routing remains unchanged pending acceptance.
why were we visiting the node multiple times? did you fix it correctly/generally or just patch the symptom?

The confirmation build is finished and tests are running without failures so far. I’ve also started the scale checks and the exact #2767 workload on the same binary. The workload is building fresh facts in the dedicated Optane cache; it is not upgrading the old cache.

I’m checking the traversal and the fix against your question. “Duplicate AST visit” may have been imprecise: lowering a call can consume its child’s reference before the normal walk reaches that child. I’ll verify that the guard handles that general case without suppressing genuinely missing references.

The fix addresses the cause, but my “duplicate visit” description was wrong.

For `service.method(arg())`, entering the call lowers the `method` child using the call’s context and records its exact AST node ID in `handled_identifiers`. The walk then descends normally—it must still find receiver and argument references, including `arg()`.

Ordinary identifier handlers already respected that bookkeeping. The field-identifier handler didn’t, so it incorrectly reported the already-emitted method reference as missing.

The fix is in the shared `mark_unlowered_identifier_boundary` helper: an already-handled node cannot be classified as unlowered. It neither skips traversal nor clears semantic uncertainty. Regression coverage checks both sides: method calls retain their reference without the false gap; unsupported `service.field` reads still report a gap. The broad confirmation is still running.

The full confirmation passed: 2,473/2,473 tests, plus all three scale checks. That includes the new missing-reference regression and existing tests for direct/generic method calls and calls nested inside generic arguments. The fix preserves child traversal; it corrects the inconsistent “already handled” check.

It fixes the underlying bookkeeping error. My “duplicate visit” description was inaccurate.

For `service.method(arg())`:

1. The call handler reads the `method` child, emits its reference, and marks that exact AST node handled.
2. Normal traversal subsequently reaches that child—and must continue through receivers and arguments to discover references such as `arg()`.
3. The field-identifier handler incorrectly reported `method` as unlowered, ignoring the existing handled-node bookkeeping.

The [fix is in the shared unlowered-identifier helper](/home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost2/crates/bifrost-rust/src/resolution.rs:2888), making it respect the same invariant other identifier handlers already followed. It does **not** skip subtrees or erase receiver/type uncertainty.

Validation passed: **2,473 tests and all three scale checks**, including method-reference retention, genuine unsupported field-read gaps, and nested generic-argument calls. M2/M3 remain unfinished; the exact workload is still running.

after.text: The previous turn made concrete progress: the combined gate and scale checks passed. I’ll check the running exact workload, then continue closing the remaining M2/M3 gaps.

The exact workload exposed another M2 blocker: several real source files exceed the publication row limit. I’ve delegated that batching investigation. In parallel, I’m preparing the usage-result bound
publication row limit? why is that a thing?

I’m checking why that limit was introduced. The important distinction is between a batch-size target and a hard limit on one source file; those appear to be coupled here. No limit change has been made

It’s a Bifrost-imposed limit on **one write transaction**, not a SQLite limit or a maximum database size.  The current setting—400,000 rows, 32 MiB of payload, up to 256 blobs—came from writer-through
